seo.title: Karmic tail 21 7 13 compatibility: The World, The Chariot, Death
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 7 13 compatibility: a dream of a whole world, a chariot on the road and Death as the task: end the old life, not change the address.

title: The couple's karmic tail 21-7-13: a world sought in a change of place
short: The three cards of the couple's tail 21-7-13 read like an itinerary: The World is travel and moving abroad, The Chariot is the vehicle, Death is the end of the line. It looks like a one-way ticket, but the tail reads the other way round. The couple enters the task with a shared picture of a whole, proper life waiting for them somewhere else, and they head for it on anything that moves. Yet the main task, Death, asks them to end the old shape of the union where they stand: not to change the address, but to change the life.

sections.h2: A novella about a couple who keep leaving
paragraphs: Chekhov finished The Duel in the summer of 1891 on the Bogimovo estate. Ivan Andreitch Laevsky, a civil servant of about twenty-eight, and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna, another man's wife, left Petersburg two years earlier for a small seaside town in the Caucasus. The novella opens with Laevsky standing shoulder-deep in the sea, asking his friend Samoylenko, an army medic, what to do once you have stopped loving. It closes with the two of them staying on the same shore: married, poor and, it seems, alive for the first time.

Why this novella? Its plot runs in the same order as the three cards. First the dream of a whole world for which they left. Then endless plans to leave and the duel itself — The Chariot. At the end, the night before the shot and the morning when the old life is over and nobody has died. Even the number fits: the novella has exactly twenty-one chapters. That is a coincidence, not proof, but it makes the tail easier to remember.

sections.h2: The World at the entry: one dream, two pictures
paragraphs: What does a 21-7-13 couple want together? Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, describes the entry point as the couple's wishes and agreements, its "common language". The World here is the wish for a whole life: not to fix one thing, but to start everything at once and properly, preferably somewhere else. For Laevsky the dream sounds almost like a plan: "We pictured our future like this: to begin with, in the Caucasus, while we were getting to know the people and the place, I would put on the Government uniform and enter the service; then at our leisure we would pick out a plot of ground, would toil in the sweat of our brow, would have a vineyard and a field, and so on."

Four chapters later Chekhov shows the same dream through Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's eyes, and it is a different picture. She had imagined she "would find here on the first day a cosy nook by the sea, a snug little garden with shade, with birds, with little brooks, where she could grow flowers and vegetables, rear ducks and hens, entertain her neighbours". He saw a vineyard, a field and toil in the sweat of his brow. She saw a little garden, ducks and neighbours. They travelled to one world and never once compared the pictures.

When the world failed to happen, the couple came to an agreement — in silence. Chekhov writes that "they seemed to be in a tacit compact never to allude to a life of hard work". This is how the entry point becomes resistance: the couple's common language turns into a common silence. She is sure he is angry with her over the life of labour that never came, and her reasoning goes one step further: "He was silent about it, she thought, because he was angry with her for being silent about it." Each carries the guilt for a dream they never talked through.

For a couple today it need not be a move to the sea. It can be "once we buy the house", "once we leave, everything will settle", "once the renovation is done, we will really live". The World at the entry is never modest: it promises everything at once. And while it stays a picture, it can be neither tested nor corrected.

The dream of a whole world has a reverse side, which Lisovskaya describes as routine and "Groundhog Day". In the novella it can be heard in one line at dinner: "The same thing every day." The zoologist Von Koren lays out Laevsky's day by the hour: "in the morning, slippers, a bathe, and coffee; then till dinner-time, slippers, a constitutional, and conversation…" The whole world has shrunk to a timetable, and once more the whole world seems to be wherever the couple is not: "he conceived that wonderful world as real and possible, not on this sea-front… but there in the North". Two years ago salvation was the Caucasus; now it is Petersburg.

The novella also has the plain words. Laevsky says of Nadyezhda Fyodorovna that she "has followed you to the ends of the earth". The couple already stands at the edge of the world and still looks for it further on.

sections.h2: The letter in the pocket: an ending that has already come
paragraphs: In the very first chapter Laevsky has a secret: two days earlier a letter arrived saying that Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's husband has died. He hides it: "To show her that letter would be equivalent to 'Come to church to be married.' And we should first have to make our relations clear."

This is the tail's main task, arriving before anything else. Death in the couple's main task is not about people dying but about a form coming to an end. The life the couple had been living as if provisionally, for the time being, ended on the day the letter came. The old obstacle is gone, and now they will have to choose: make the union official or part honestly. Both of them stall.

He carries the letter in his pocket, the letter "which he had been intending every day to read to her", as Chekhov puts it. She, once she knows, answers Marya Konstantinovna, who is already eager to play matchmaker: "What should we be married for? I see no necessity for it. We'll go on living as we have lived." He wants to end the union and she wants to keep it as it was, yet both resist the same thing — a change of form. The World at the entry wants everything to stay "as we have lived", only better. Death replies that "as we have lived" is already over.

For a couple today such a letter can be any news that changes the shape of the union: a divorce finalised, a job offer in another city, an inheritance, the sale of a parent's flat, a talk about children. The trap of the 21-7-13 tail is that news like this is easy to carry in a pocket. It is put off not out of malice but in order to "make our relations clear first". Yet it is exactly this news that makes them clear.

sections.h2: The Chariot in the middle: an escape for each
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple lives the road from the dream to the ending. In this tail the middle is The Chariot, and in The Duel it never stops moving. In the second chapter alone Laevsky says the same words seven times: "Run away!" His imagination lays out the route to the last station: "he would go aboard the steamer and then would have some lunch, would drink some cold beer… then would get into the train at Sevastopol and set off. Hurrah for freedom! …then Kursk, Moscow…"

Chekhov names exactly how the road replaces thought: "He would get into the train and set off, and thereby the problem of his life would be solved, and he did not let his thoughts go farther." The Chariot at its worst is not speed. It is the belief that motion will settle by itself what has to be settled in words.

The subtlest thing in the novella is that there is more than one escape. Nadyezhda Fyodorovna, tangled in debts and in a secret of her own, also decides to leave: "I am going away. Ivan Andreitch may stay, but I am going." She thinks of going away from him secretly, living in some remote place and sending him money "anonymously". He means to leave alone and send for her later. Two people under one roof are plotting two separate routes and not telling each other about them.

Even to the picnic the couple rides separately: he in a char-à-banc with Samoylenko, she in a coach with the ladies. On the way back, after his rude remark, they climb into different carriages, each with strangers. The couple has a chariot, but each rides in it alone.

The central question of the middle is spoken aloud in the novella. Samoylenko, who is scraping together money for Laevsky's journey, asks: "why shouldn't you take Nadyezhda Fyodorovna with you?" — "You queer fellow. How is that possible? One of us must stay, or our creditors will raise an outcry." Among the couple's tasks for The Chariot Lisovskaya lists exactly this one: to make up their minds to move together. Not to move as such, but to move together. The Chariot in this tail asks not "where to" but "the two of us?"

Laevsky borrows the money for the journey, and Lisovskaya puts loans and dodging responsibility on the negative side of The Chariot. It is recognisable without the Caucasus: an escape hatch for each, talk of moving in which "we" means "me now, you later", one partner bending to the other's plans instead of a shared decision.

sections.h2: The duel: a war that drives the wrong way
paragraphs: The Chariot is a card of motion and victory, and Waite's list of its meanings includes war. But in The Duel the couple does not fight each other. The tension goes outwards. Laevsky snaps not at Nadyezhda Fyodorovna but at Samoylenko and at Von Koren, who has long despised him: "I will fight you!" — and the zoologist accepts the challenge. Waite's reversed Chariot reads "Riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat". All of it fits into one scene in a drawing-room, and that evening Von Koren is already asking what the penalty for a duel would be.

Von Koren explains the mechanics of The Chariot better than any commentator: "we shall not stop, we shall go there and fight. So there is some force stronger than our reasoning." Laevsky, for his part, sees the duel as one more means of transport: "this duel was so far good in that it made it impossible for Laevsky to remain in the town afterwards." Even a shot is a way out of town for him.

For a 21-7-13 couple this is a familiar substitution: instead of talking to each other, a battle with the outside world. With relatives, with neighbours, with work, with the town that is "to blame for everything". A war outside gives a sense of motion, but it solves the wrong problem.
They fight where the picnic was held: by Kerbalay's duhan, where the Black River meets the Yellow. The road on which the couple so often meant to leave brings them back to the same spot.

sections.h2: The night before the shot: the death that did not happen
paragraphs: The tail's main task is Death, and Lisovskaya reads this point mainly through its negative side: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. In The Duel the lesson takes one night. On the eve of the duel Laevsky learns Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's secret, the one she had kept quiet about. At night a storm breaks. He sits down at the table: "On the eve of death one ought to write to one's nearest relation."

The first word of the letter is "Mother!" His mother had never forgiven him this liaison, and all his plans of escape rested on her money and on lying to her. He wants to beg his mother to give Nadyezhda Fyodorovna shelter and warmth — and crosses the word out. Then he writes it again several more times. Among the couple's tasks for Death, Lisovskaya puts first helping each other to separate from their parents. Here it happens literally: a man crosses out the hope that his parent's home will decide things for him.

Towards morning Laevsky arrives at the thought for which the novella seems to have been written: "the man who seeks salvation in change of place like a migrating bird would find nothing anywhere, for all the world is alike to him." It is a verdict not on the Caucasus and not on Petersburg, but on the itinerary. The World at the entry promised salvation somewhere else. Death in the main task answers that the place decides nothing.

Before getting into the carriage he goes into the bedroom. Nadyezhda Fyodorovna starts up in bed and says she expected him to "turn me out of the house into the rain and storm, but you delay . . . delay . . .". He takes her in his arms and realises that she is "the one creature near and dear to him, whom no one could replace". Then comes a short sentence on which the whole tail rests: "When he went out of the house and got into the carriage he wanted to return home alive." For the first time the chariot is not driving away but holding a return ticket.

Chekhov builds the morning of the duel on the words "for the first time in his life". Von Koren sees green rays at sunrise for the first time in his life. Laevsky "saw the sunrise now for the first time in his life". The young officers acting as seconds are at a duel for the first time, and nobody present knows how a duel is done. Death in this tail is an experience the couple has not had before: further down it turns out that 13 appears in neither partner's personal tail.

Von Koren aims at the forehead. The deacon, who has crept along to watch, shouts from the maize: "He'll kill him!" — and the bullet only grazes the neck. Nobody has died. But on the drive home it seems to Laevsky "as though they were all coming back from a graveyard in which a wearisome, insufferable man who was a burden to others had just been buried". "Everything is over," he thinks of his past. This is Death at its best: what dies is not a person but a way of living that could not go on.

And at home comes a scene Lisovskaya would call the positive side of the thirteenth energy: the couple accepts each other's past and moves on. Nadyezhda Fyodorovna hurries to tell him everything and fears he will curse her, "but he listened to her, stroked her face and hair, looked into her eyes and said: 'I have nobody but you. . . .'"

sections.h2: What Waite and Wen see: "change of place"
paragraphs: Arthur Waite's list of meanings for The World sounds like a steamship timetable: "Assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place." It ends on change of place. In 1916 Constance Garnett translated The Duel into English, and Laevsky's night thought came out in her version in those very words: "the man who seeks salvation in change of place like a migrating bird would find nothing anywhere, for all the world is alike to him". The words that close Waite's list for The World are exactly what Laevsky gives up on the night before the duel. And where Chekhov wrote zemlya vezde odinakova, "the earth is the same everywhere", Garnett wrote "all the world".

Waite's reversed World ends with the words "stagnation, permanence" — the very Groundhog Day people run from. The World at the entry holds both extremes at once: to tear oneself away and to freeze on the spot. Either one lets a couple avoid changing the shape of its life.

Benebell Wen describes the reversed World almost as a scene from the first chapter: "there was a major change presented in the Seeker's life that could have been great for the Seeker's future, but the Seeker is afraid of change and is hesitating to take the necessary actions"; the Seeker may be "consciously and knowingly in denial". The letter in Laevsky's pocket and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's "we'll go on living as we have lived" are both versions at once.

Of Death, Wen writes that the card is "a call to let go of the present and move on". To move on is not to move away. The World tempts the couple to change the place; Death asks it to change the stage. The difference is one word, and the whole tail stands on it.

One more detail comes from Wen's description of The Chariot as drawn in the Rider-Waite-Smith deck: in front of the chariot are "two sphinxes, one dark and one light". In The Duel both the picnic and the shot happen where the Black River falls into the Yellow and "the water black as ink stains the yellow and struggles with it". Time after time the couple's carriage arrives at the place where two different forces contend in one channel.

sections.h2: Justice at the centre: a couple forever being weighed
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is the atmosphere, what lies between the partners and is not on show. Every couple with the tail 21-7-13 has the same card there: 8, Justice. No exceptions. And The Duel is a novella about a couple who are weighed all the time.

Everyone judges them. Von Koren considers Laevsky harmful and reminds his listeners that "People are judged by their actions". Marya Konstantinovna tells Nadyezhda Fyodorovna, "At the bottom of my heart I blamed you", and demands a wedding. On his way to the duel the deacon asks a question fit to be the motto of the eighth arcanum: "By what standard must one measure men's qualities, to judge rightly of them?" And the two judge themselves most harshly of all: he asks whether it is his fault that her husband died; she feels "hopelessly guilty towards him".

The other side of Justice is the ledger. In the novella money is counted all the time. Laevsky owes about two thousand roubles; he already owes Samoylenko about four hundred and asks for three hundred more to leave. Nadyezhda Fyodorovna owes three hundred roubles at Atchmianov's shop, and in delirium she repeats: "At first a hundred . . . then another hundred . . . and then the third hundred. . . ." Even the medic at the duel names his fee: "Each side is to pay me fifteen roubles, and in the case of the death of one party, the survivor is to pay thirty."

For Lisovskaya, Justice in a couple's atmosphere means a wish to make the relationship official and an honest division of duties; on the negative side come reluctance to marry, broken promises, debts and the habit of blaming instead of admitting one's own fault. It reads almost like the table of contents of The Duel. And almost like instructions for its ending: in the last chapter Laevsky is married, and "He sits from morning till night, he's always at work. He works to pay off his debts."

Here is the tail's most beautiful arithmetic. Justice at the centre plus Death in the main task give The World at the entry: 8 + 13 = 21. The world the couple dreams of is made of two terms: an honest ledger and the end of the old life. That is exactly the world Laevsky and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna receive at the end — not a vineyard and not a garden with ducks, but a wedding, work to pay the debts and "the little house with three windows" in the same small town. It is smaller than the dream. But it is real.
Justice at the centre does not mean that one of the two is right. The harshest judge in the novella, Von Koren, says as he leaves: "No one knows the real truth."

sections.h2: The numbers: what every such couple shares
paragraphs: The tail 21-7-13 occurs in about one couple in 148 (0.677%) and ranks 50th of the 97 couple tails. Each point of the couple's chart is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts; a sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. This tail arises from only three combinations of the partners' personal tails.

**The Chariot in the middle is born only in the couple.** Neither partner has it in the middle of a personal tail: there you find The Sun and The Devil, The Tower and The Moon, or Judgement and Temperance. The couple's middle is exactly 34 every time, and 34 reduces to 7. And 34 = 21 + 13: the middle of a personal tail is the sum of its two ends, so the couple's middle adds up the entry and the main task. This is not a metaphor but the way the numbers are built: the road of this couple is made of the dream and the ending. Laevsky would put it more briefly — on the train "the problem of his life would be solved".

**The World at the entry is made of two retreats.** In 96% of such couples the entry is built from one partner's Hanged Man and the other's Hermit: 12 + 9. Our reading: a pause, life on hold, and a withdrawal into one's own territory are two ways of stepping back from the world, and together they produce the dream of a whole world. Laevsky and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna live "on this empty, desolate coast, always expecting something better" — the pause and the solitude at once. In the remaining 4% the entry is The Devil plus The Lovers, 15 + 6.

**Death is new to both of them.** The main task is always an exact sum — 7 + 6, 4 + 9 or 5 + 8 — and 13 appears in neither partner's personal tail. In 92% of couples the couple's Death is made of one partner's personal Chariot (that tail ends in 7) and the other's personal Lovers: of a road and a choice. In the novella the end of the old life comes exactly so: from the drive to the duel and the choice made at the bedside that morning.

**The centre is always 8.** And 13 + 8 = 21, 21 + 13 = 34 → 7: in this tail the couple's arithmetic matches the personal one. That is why the same order 21-7-13 also occurs as a personal tail, for 678 dates since 1900. But that is a different calculation with different roles for the points; this page is only about the couple's tail. Here too the couple's middle is not recalculated from the ends: it remains the sum of two personal middles, and the result simply coincides.
There are no permutations of this tail: no other couple tails are made of the numbers 21, 7 and 13.
Two dates that give the couple's tail 21-7-13. First each person's own chart is calculated, then the matching points are added.

This couple's values card is 6, The Lovers. And The World appears in its chart in one more place: in the sphere "What can spoil it", at the point "Where it sparks". The dream at the entry is here also a source of quarrels. That is a feature of this one couple, not of every couple with the tail 21-7-13.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. Couples with the tail 21-7-13 have one of two cards here: The Lovers in 75.8% and The Devil in 24.2%. Both are about the bond between two people, but the knot is different. The Lovers are held together by choice. The Devil by attachment: habit, debt, the fear of being left alone. Lisovskaya ends her chapter on the fifteenth energy with the thought that no one belongs to anyone.

The Duel has both knots. At first Laevsky speaks of Nadyezhda Fyodorovna as of an object: he is for her "an indispensable, integral part of her boudoir", and it would be as hard for her to do without him "as to do without her powder or her curl-papers". Von Koren describes his life as a "narrow programme" within which his existence is confined "like an egg within its shell". That is the language of The Devil. At dawn before the duel the language of The Lovers is heard: "the one creature near and dear to him, whom no one could replace". The same person, the same house, a different knot.

Wen distinguishes The Lovers from Justice like this: "The Lovers is about making an ethical decision that involves the Seeker", while Justice "is about making an ethical decision that involves an external condition, others who matter to the Seeker, or a situation outside of the Seeker." For this tail it is an exact map of the ground. At the couple's centre stands judgement and reckoning from outside, the eight. In its values stands a decision only the two of them can make, the six. However much the neighbours, duellists and creditors judge, the decision is still theirs.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: a boat that takes two steps forward
paragraphs: In the last chapter Von Koren leaves. Laevsky and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna stay exactly where they had spent two years planning to escape from. Laevsky sees the zoologist off at the quay and watches the boat being flung about on the waves: "she makes two steps forward and one step back; but the boatmen are stubborn, they work the oars unceasingly, and are not afraid of the high waves." And he thinks: "So it is in life. . . ."

This is The Chariot at its best. Not a carriage to Petersburg and not a steamer out of here, but a boat rowed by several people at once, against the waves, towards lights that cannot yet be seen. The tail 21-7-13 does not require the couple to stay put. It asks that the motion be shared and that it not take the place of ending what has already ended.

ul: **Compare the pictures of the dream.** Say aloud what "our new life" looks like for each of you: a vineyard and a field, or a little garden with ducks and neighbours. The World at the entry is sturdier when there is one picture for two, not two silent ones.
**Do not carry the letter in a pocket.** News that changes the shape of the union is told the same day. It cannot be "made clear first": it is the clarification itself.

**One route for two.** Plans to leave, to move to a new city or take a new job are discussed as shared plans. "I'll go now, you'll come later" is a sign that the chariot is once again carrying one person at a time.

**Tell a change of place from a change of life.** Before a big step, ask each other what exactly has to end. If the answer is "everything here", it is worth checking whether that "everything" would leave together with the suitcases.

**Keep the ledger together.** Debts, promises and grievances out loud and on a list, not in one's head and not in delirium. Justice at the centre works for the couple when the two of them keep the accounts, not the neighbours.
**Bury the past, not each other.** The end of the old shape of a union is not a verdict on the union. Sometimes, as in The Duel, only after such an ending does a couple have its first real day.

paragraphs: Chekhov promises his characters no happiness. Von Koren, saying goodbye, thinks: "What pitiful figures they are, though! The life they are living does not come easy to them." But this life is theirs, and for the first time it is not somewhere else. That is the secret of the tail 21-7-13: the whole world the couple travels towards turns out to be not a place on the map but the next chapter. And it can only begin where the previous one ended.

ul: **21 · The World — entry to the task.** Where the couple starts: a dream of a whole world for two, a life in which everything finally falls into place. The same dream turns into resistance when life refuses to match the picture.
**7 · The Chariot — middle of the task.** How the couple travels: by motion, plans, departures and a struggle for the reins. Here the road easily takes the place of a conversation.

**13 · Death — main task.** What there is to learn: to let what is worn out come to an end — the provisional way of living, the unspoken agreements, the hope that a parent's home will sort things out — and to start the next chapter together.

intro: About one couple in 148 has this tail. It is best explained not by a textbook but by Chekhov's novella The Duel: the story of two people who ran away to the ends of the earth for a new life and spent two years planning to run away again.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-7-13 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's tasks read in the order "entry to the task — middle — main task". The couple enters with a dream of a whole world (21, The World), lives the road through motion, plans and struggle (7, The Chariot), and learns the main lesson: to let a worn-out shape of life and union come to an end (13, Death).

faq.q: Is Death in a couple's main task a sign of a break-up?
faq.a: No. The card speaks of the end of a form, not of people and not of the union: old agreements, a provisional way of living, the hope that a parent's home will help. The number does not predict events. In The Duel the only shot that could have killed missed, and what ended was the couple's former life.

faq.q: Does a couple with the tail 21-7-13 have to move?
faq.a: No. In this tail a move can be both a task and a trap. Among the couple's tasks for The Chariot Lisovskaya lists making up their minds to move together, and the key word is "together". The trap is expecting a new place to settle by itself what has to be ended.

faq.q: How does the couple's tail 21-7-13 differ from the personal tail 21-7-13?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date and describes one person's tasks; its points have different roles. A couple's tail is the sum of the points of two personal charts, and the partners themselves have other tails: in 92% of such couples they are 12-19-7 and 9-15-6.

faq.q: How common is the tail 21-7-13 among couples?
faq.a: About one couple in 148: that is 0.677% of couples and 50th place among the 97 couple tails. Every such couple has Justice at the centre, and in the values either The Lovers (75.8%) or The Devil (24.2%).

Laevsky and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna left Petersburg for the Caucasus in search of a whole, proper life. That is The World at the entry: the wish to start everything at once, preferably somewhere else. His picture: "we would pick out a plot of ground, would toil in the sweat of our brow, would have a vineyard and a field, and so on". Her picture, four chapters later: "a snug little garden with shade, with birds, with little brooks… rear ducks and hens, entertain her neighbours". report.h3: An ending carried in a pocket

report: In the first chapter a letter arrives: Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's husband has died. Laevsky hides it: "To show her that letter would be equivalent to 'Come to church to be married.'" Once she knows, she says: "We'll go on living as we have lived." He wants to end the union and she wants to keep it as it was, yet both resist the same thing — a change of form. Death in the couple's main task is not about people dying but about a form coming to an end: the provisional life ended on the day of the letter. For a couple today such a letter can be any news that changes the way they live, and it is far too easy to carry in a pocket.

The middle of the task is The Chariot, and in the novella it never stops moving. In the second chapter Laevsky says "Run away!" seven times. Chekhov names exactly how the road stands in for thought: "He would get into the train and set off, and thereby the problem of his life would be solved, and he did not let his thoughts go farther."

report.h3: The death that did not happen

report: On the night before the duel Laevsky writes "Mother!" and crosses it out: the hope that his parent's home will decide things for him comes to an end. Towards morning he reaches the central thought of the novella: "the man who seeks salvation in change of place like a migrating bird would find nothing anywhere, for all the world is alike to him." Waite's list of meanings for The World ends with the very same words, "change of place". And in Constance Garnett's English translation Laevsky's night thought comes out exactly so: "seeks salvation in change of place". The World at the entry promised salvation somewhere else. Death answers that the place decides nothing.

Before the shot he takes Nadyezhda Fyodorovna in his arms and realises that she is "the one creature near and dear to him, whom no one could replace", and as he gets into the carriage he wants to "return home alive". The bullet only grazes his neck. Nobody has died, yet on the drive home it seems to Laevsky as though they are all "coming back from a graveyard in which a wearisome, insufferable man who was a burden to others had just been buried". **What dies is not a person but a way of living.** At home she hurries to tell him everything, and he listens and says: "I have nobody but you. . . ."

report.h3: A world made of a ledger and an ending

report: Every couple with this tail has Justice at the centre, and the novella is full of scales. The neighbours and the zoologist judge the couple, the two judge themselves most harshly of all, and money is counted to the rouble: debts, loans for the journey, three hundred owed at a shop. Justice at the centre plus Death in the main task give The World at the entry: 8 + 13 = 21. **The world the couple dreams of is made of an honest ledger and the end of the old life.** That is the world the two receive at the end: not a vineyard and not a garden with ducks, but a wedding, work to pay off the debts and "the little house with three windows" in the same small town. It is smaller than the dream, but it is real.

The last picture in the novella is a boat in a storm: "she makes two steps forward and one step back; but the boatmen are stubborn". This is The Chariot at its best, when the motion is shared and does not take the place of ending what has already ended. Simple things change the pattern: comparing the two pictures of the dream out loud; telling news that changes the shape of the union the same day; making plans to leave as shared plans, without "I'll go now, you'll come later"; asking before a big step what exactly has to end; keeping the ledger together, not in one's head.
The secret of the tail 21-7-13 is that **the whole world turns out to be not a place on the map but the next chapter**. And it can only begin where the previous one ended.
